headline_marked: FIFA to decide on [[Argentina's Falklands banner]] after England clash
headline: FIFA to decide on Argentina's Falklands banner after England clash
summary: The governing body is assessing match reports after players displayed a political banner claiming the islands are Argentine following a 2-1 victory.
details: Argentina's football team displayed a banner reading "Las Malvinas son Argentinas" (The Falklands are Argentine) after their 2-1 win over England in a World Cup semi-final match in Atlanta.

FIFA's independent disciplinary committee is currently assessing match reports to determine if any action will be taken based on the FIFA disciplinary code, which bans political symbols on the field of play.
British Business Minister Peter Kyle and Downing Street have called the gesture an "egregious violation" of rules, asserting that the Falkland Islands belong to Britain.
Argentina President Javier Milei defended the stunt as "perfectly valid and legitimate," stating that the nation intends to recover the islands through diplomatic means.
The dispute dates back to a 1982 conflict between the two nations, which resulted in the deaths of 649 Argentines and 255 Britons.
In 2014, the Argentine football association was fined £20,000 for a similar gesture before a friendly match against Slovenia.
Tensions have escalated further with Argentina's Foreign Minister Pablo Quirno filing a formal protest over the passage of a British warship, HMS Medway, through Argentine waters.
caption:
A political banner at the World Cup sparks a diplomatic row. Will FIFA penalize Argentina?

Argentina's football team displayed a banner reading "Las Malvinas son Argentinas" (The Falklands are Argentine) after their 2-1 win over England in a World Cup semi-final match in Atlanta.

FIFA's independent disciplinary committee is currently assessing match reports to determine if any action will be taken based on the FIFA disciplinary code, which bans political symbols on the field of play.

British Business Minister Peter Kyle and Downing Street have called the gesture an "egregious violation" of rules, asserting that the Falkland Islands belong to Britain.

Argentina President Javier Milei defended the stunt as "perfectly valid and legitimate," stating that the nation intends to recover the islands through diplomatic means.

The dispute dates back to a 1982 conflict between the two nations, which resulted in the deaths of 649 Argentines and 255 Britons.

In 2014, the Argentine football association was fined £20,000 for a similar gesture before a friendly match against Slovenia.

Tensions have escalated further with Argentina's Foreign Minister Pablo Quirno filing a formal protest over the passage of a British warship, HMS Medway, through Argentine waters.

Source: The Daily Star
